Noah M.
Daniels I ask you to consider my candidacy for the Faculty Senate Executive Committee for a 2-year term, 2026-2028.
I am an associate professor of computer science, and will have been a member of the faculty for 10 years as of Fall 2026.
I am beginning my second term on the Faculty Senate, and just completing my first 1-year term on FSEC.
In my first term on Faculty Senate, I served two years as chair of the Committee on Technology and Infrastructure.
In that time, my primary focus was on developing consensus policies for ITS to replace unilaterally-developed policies set forth by the administration which hindered academic freedom, research, and teaching.
I have continued this effort as the FSEC liaison to CTI.
This has culminated in a draft of the new ITS policy (with several flaws noted by the faculty) presented for comment in the last month.

In my time on CTI and FSEC, I have served on the IT Governance committee, on the search committees for the Chief Information Officer as well as the University Librarian, and am a founding member of the ad-hoc committees to proactively evaluate whether the technologies on which we depend are effective before the administration signs lengthy contracts.
I enjoy bringing my own perspective to these intellectually diverse working groups, and reconciling that perspective with those of others.
I see the particular strengths I bring to FSEC as including a deep understanding of both technology and how people use technology, as well as a bulwark to efforts to corporatize university ITS and other aspects of university life.
In a tumultuous time when new cybersecurity threats lead to sometimes-draconian policies that can impact research and teaching, as well as the rise of “AI” everywhere (sometimes without the needed critical thinking), I believe I can bring expertise and reasoned argument to addressing these issues.
Beyond technology, I see the adoption of the new budget model and the recent, eye-opening budget committee survey as being a key concern of FSEC going forward.
I believe we must work with the administration to address specific concerns brought to light by that survey, outreach to faculty, and other data such as the explosion of new course proposals. 1
